think:
1. Core Clinical Tension: A 14-year-old male presents with acute fever followed on day 3 by dramatic cerebellar and brainstem signs: spontaneous ocular flutter, titubation, and gait ataxia. While opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome, acute cerebellitis, or brainstem encephalitis are primary neurologic considerations, concurrent systemic thrombocytopenia and transaminitis point toward a parainfectious neuro-ophthalmologic complication of an acute arboviral infection.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The triage presentation concludes after the 3-day history of fever, headache, and vomiting, physical exam demonstrating ocular flutter, titubation, ataxia, and mild hepatosplenomegaly, and initial triage labs showing thrombocytopenia and transaminitis, immediately prior to send-out arboviral serologies, brain MRI, and lumbar puncture.
3. Differential Distinctions: Acute cerebellitis or opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia syndrome typically occurs as an isolated autoimmune syndrome without marked systemic thrombocytopenia or hepatitis and often exhibits limb myoclonus; primary viral meningoencephalitis produces altered sensorium and abnormal CSF findings, both absent here.
case_prompt: A 14-year-old male presented with a 3-day history of fever associated with chills, continuous holocranial headache, and 3 to 4 episodes of vomiting. On the third day of illness, he noted acute giddiness, difficulty sitting and standing independently requiring family support, and swaying while walking. He also reported blurred vision, but denied dysphagia, dysarthria, limb weakness, sensory disturbance, or myoclonic jerks. On physical examination, vital signs were stable. He was conscious and oriented with normal speech. Pupils were equal and reactive to light. Oculomotor examination revealed sudden conjugate horizontal saccadic oscillations without an intersaccadic interval (ocular flutter), occurring spontaneously with eyes both open and closed, during visual pursuit and saccades. Other cranial nerves were intact. Motor examination demonstrated normal tone and power with sluggish deep tendon reflexes and mute plantar responses. Sensory examination was normal. He exhibited titubation along with truncal, stance, and gait ataxia. Abdominal examination revealed mild hepatosplenomegaly. Initial laboratory studies revealed a platelet count of 76,000/mcL (0.76 lakh) and elevated liver transaminases (AST 110 IU/L, ALT 156 IU/L).

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered due to the explosive onset of rapid horizontal saccadic oscillations and severe truncal ataxia; ruled out as an isolated post-infectious autoimmune syndrome by the acute concurrent presence of viremic hallmarks (thrombocytopenia, hepatosplenomegaly, transaminitis), lack of limb myoclonus, and normal CSF analysis.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: There was blurring of vision but no dysphagia, dysarthria, weakness or incoordination of limbs, sensory symptoms, or myoclonic jerks.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered because of acute fever, headache, vomiting, and ataxia; ruled out by preserved orientation, normal brain MRI without parenchymal abnormalities, and entirely normal CSF analysis.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Magnetic resonance imaging brain plain was normal. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis was normal.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: The diagnostic turning point was identifying acute parainfectious ocular flutter and ataxia occurring alongside hallmark systemic thrombocytopenia (76,000/mcL) and transaminitis, confirmed by positive serum NS1 antigen and IgM antibodies, followed by rapid steroid-responsive recovery.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Serum dengue nonstructural 1 antigen and immunoglobulin M antibodies were positive.

editor_comments: Distilled strictly to emergency admission triage. Rare parainfectious ocular flutter and truncal ataxia in an acute febrile child; confirmed by NS1 antigen and IgM serology.
